items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Tell us about some of your duo work with Joe Pass. ... I loved him and he was my favorite guitarist and still is. And we had a way of playing. We could play, we knew how to back each other up

ctx.x: Well I just would like to ask you then, if you would give us a word of wisdom, if you had a word to say to young guitarists coming up, wanting to involve themselves in this music. What would it be?

You mean musically? I would tell them that it’s necessary, vital that they learn to play what they sing. You know when you’re humming along with what you’re playing you know. Joe Pass did it. Wes Montgomery did it. Clark Terry does it — all the good — Oscar does it, Ray Brown does it. Anybody who plays, you can’t tell horn players, © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

because they’ve got something in their mouth. But ask them, and they’re playing what they’re singing, you know? And that way you make your own music, see? Because you’re singing it. And another thing, you won’t sing a bunch of silly stuff. You might play a bunch of silly stuff, but you won’t sing about [scats] and so it really is the one thing that I say is absolutely vital.

items.title: Herb Ellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I first did them with Joe Pass... we both played Donte’s in Los Angeles

ctx.x: When did it occur to you to start doing these great duet records with other guitar players?
Gosh. Well I first did them with Joe Pass. And I don’t know how that came about. But we both played Donte’s in Los Angeles you know, at different times.
